stops.name: Konya, the funeral of every faith
stops.campa: Word of the death runs through Konya faster than the criers can carry it, and the funeral the next day draws, the tradition insists, not only Muslims but the city's Christians and Jews into the same weeping crowd, each reading aloud from their own scripture as the bier passes. Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, Ibn al-Arabi's own stepson and Rumi's neighbor of many years, is given the honor of leading the funeral prayer, but is so overcome, some say by a vision of the Prophet and his angels walking the procession, that he faints before it is finished, and Husam al-Din Chelebi completes the prayer in his place.

stops.name: Konya, burial beneath the Green Dome
stops.campa: Rumi is laid in the ground beside his father in the Sultan's rose garden, and over the grave the city, and later the Seljuk and Karamanid and Ottoman patrons who follow, raise the tower of glazed turquoise tile the whole world will come to know as the Green Dome, the Kubbe-i Hadra. Ala al-Din Kayqubad's madrasa around it becomes, in time, a lodge, then a museum, then again, quietly, a place of pilgrimage regardless of what any government has called it. The dome still stands over both graves, father and son, sea and the ocean that outgrew it, in the same small plot of Konya earth.

stops.name: Konya, Husam al-Din Chelebi, the first regent of the order
stops.campa: By Rumi's own wish, spoken before his death, Husam al-Din Chelebi, the scribe of the Masnavi, takes his place at the head of the disciples: the first postnishin, the one who sits on the sheepskin, of what has not yet a name of its own but will become the Mevlevi order. For ten years he holds the circle together, dictating nothing new, only guarding what has been dictated, until his own death passes the seat briefly to another elder disciple, Karim al-Din Baktamur, before it comes, as the blood and the poetry both intended all along, to Rumi's own son.

stops.name: Konya, Sultan Walad braids the order and the rite of the turning
stops.campa: Sultan Walad, the boy once sent to Damascus to fetch Shams home, becomes at last the full head of the brotherhood his father never formally founded, and does what his father, lost always in the poem and the turning, never had time to do: gives the sema a fixed order of movements, the black cloak shed for the white, the tall camel-hair hat raised like a tombstone, the arms crossed and then opened to sky and earth; writes his own Ibtidanama and Rabab-nama to keep the story straight for pupils who never saw Shams; and sends the first Mevlevi lodges outward from Konya along the roads his grandfather once fled down in the other direction.

stops.name: From Konya to Sarajevo and Galata, the order's far branches
stops.campa: The turning outlives every empire that hosts it: Seljuk, Karamanid, six centuries of Ottoman patronage, lodges rising from Cairo to Aleppo to Sarajevo to the domed hall at Galata above the Bosphorus, each teaching the same forty-day cell, the same reed-cry, the same wheel of the arms. In 1925 the new Republic closes every tekke by law, Konya's own included; the dervishes turn in secret, or not at all, for decades, until UNESCO names the sema a Masterpiece of Humanity's Heritage in 2005, and the wheel turns openly again — at the Hadži Sinan tekke where a Sarajevo boy once watched it, at the Galata house where a seeker once had its mathematics explained to him.
